analysis.one_liner: Requires electronics makers to share repair parts, tools, and manuals with independent repair shops and owners.
analysis.headline: The Senate's right-to-repair bill has sat in the Commerce Committee since February 2026 with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Repair Act would require makers of digital electronics — phones, laptops, appliances, and anything else that depends on digital parts — to sell documentation, parts, and repair tools to independent repair shops and equipment owners on the same terms they give their own authorized repairers. It would also ban software "parts pairing" tricks that disable a device when a non-original part is installed. The FTC and state attorneys general would enforce the rules, and the bill would not apply to cars, medical devices, or off-road and farm equipment.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who own or lease electronics gain the right to fix their devices or take them to any repair shop instead of paying the manufacturer's repair prices or replacing the device. Independent repair shops gain access to the same parts, manuals, and diagnostic tools the manufacturer's authorized network gets, and used-device refurbishers could restore more equipment to full function. Sec. 2 requires parts and tools "on fair and reasonable terms" equal to the best terms given to authorized repair providers [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Owners and independent shops would be entitled to manuals, schematics, parts, and tools — including updates — at prices no worse than the manufacturer offers its authorized repairers, ending the practice of locking repair to the manufacturer's own network [S2].

The bill bans parts pairing and related software mechanisms that prevent working parts from functioning, degrade device performance after a third-party repair, or trigger false warnings about non-original parts — tactics that currently steer people back to expensive manufacturer service [S2].

Manufacturers would have to provide the documentation, tools, and parts needed to bypass and reset security locks during repair, so a broken screen or battery doesn't permanently brick a device the owner paid for [S2].

The FTC would treat violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents for injunctions, penalties, and restitution — giving ordinary people enforcement channels beyond a single federal agency [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Original equipment manufacturers — the large electronics and appliance makers — would bear the cost of supplying parts, tools, and documentation to outside repairers and would lose repair revenue and the pricing power that comes from being the only place a broken device can be fixed. Some of that cost could be passed on in device prices, and manufacturers would no longer be liable for damage, data loss, or security breaches arising from independent repairs (Sec. 5) [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill requires manufacturers to hand over tools and instructions to disable security locks, and although trade secrets stay protected, leaked repair tools or bypass instructions could create security and privacy risks for device owners [S2].

It leaves out the sectors where repair restrictions arguably bite hardest: motor vehicles, medical devices (hospital equipment), and off-road and farm equipment such as tractors are all expressly excluded, so farmers and hospitals get no new rights under this bill [S2].
Smaller manufacturers would face real compliance costs in publishing documentation, stocking parts, and building tools, which could show up in device prices [S2].

The bill gives manufacturers a broad liability shield: they could not be sued for damage, data loss, or security breaches tied to independent repairs and would not have to warranty those repairs, so consumers take on more of the risk of a botched fix [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most households the benefits — cheaper repairs, longer-lasting devices, real competition in repair — likely outweigh the costs, and the bill is drafted with care: trade secrets are preserved, authorized repair arrangements survive, and manufacturers are shielded from liability for outside repairs. The serious design weaknesses are the exclusions of cars, medical devices, and farm equipment, which carve out some of the most restriction-heavy markets, and the security-lock tools requirement, which needs careful handling. As drafted, it is a solid consumer bill with real limits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Ben Ray Luján introduced the Fair Repair Act in the Senate on February 10, 2026 [S1][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; no hearing, markup, or vote has followed [S4].
No senator from either party has signed on as a cosponsor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electronics manufacturers are better off so far — with no committee action and no cosponsors, their exclusive control over repair pricing and parts is untouched. Consumers and independent shops gain nothing until the bill actually moves.

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Repair Act and got it referred to the Commerce Committee

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote since the bill was referred on February 10, 2026

against.name: Consumer electronics manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Manufacturers of phones, computers, and appliances have historically opposed right-to-repair mandates, arguing they risk security and force disclosure of proprietary designs

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and only one senator — a Democrat — has put their name on the bill, so the partisan shape is unknown so far.

industries.note: These manufacturers currently control who can fix their devices and what repairs cost, in part through parts pairing and parts availability. The bill would force them to sell parts, tools, and documentation to anyone on their best authorized-repairer terms, cutting into repair revenue and replacement sales — though a manufacturer that justifies high repair prices with liability risk loses that argument too, since Sec. 5 shields it from repair-related liability [S2].

Shops would gain access to the same parts, manuals, diagnostic tools, and security-lock reset tools as authorized networks, letting them compete for repairs they are now locked out of. Their interest here runs directly alongside device owners' [S2].

The bill explicitly preserves manufacturers' franchise and warranty arrangements with authorized repairers (Sec. 4(3)), so their favored channel stays intact even as competition widens — they keep a contractual head start the bill protects [S2].

With parts pairing banned and parts and tools available, refurbishers could restore more used phones, laptops, and appliances to full function, expanding the supply of affordable secondhand devices [S2].

industries.industry: Motor vehicle, medical device, and off-road equipment makers
industries.note: All are expressly carved out of the bill (Sec. 4(4)-(6)), so tractor, medical equipment, and car manufacturers lose nothing and their repair restrictions remain untouched by this legislation [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee hearing or markup on the calendar, and identical right-to-repair bills having died in committee in earlier Congresses, the likely path is that this bill sits in the Commerce Committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027 without ever getting a vote.
